citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

If $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is a finite pairwise-independent family of square-integrable real random variables on a common probability space, then
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i).$$
Pairwise independence, rather than mutual independence, is sufficient. In particular, the original finite-probability-space case is included, with pairwise atom independence as in the finite-valued convention. The empty sum has variance zero.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.

derivations.claim: Every $Y_i$ has the law of $Y_1$ by [F1]. Applying [F2] to the identity map gives $\mathbb E[Y_i]=\mu$ when $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$. If $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, applying [F2] to $y\mapsto(y-\mu)^2$ also gives $\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=\sigma^2$ by [F4].
By [F6], $\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$. Linearity [F3] and step 1.1 therefore give $\mathbb E[\bar Y_n]=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E[Y_i]=\mu$.

Assume $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$. Since $|y|\le1+y^2$ for every real $y$, each $Y_i$ is integrable as well as square-integrable. The first $n$ terms are pairwise independent by [F1], so [F5] and step 1.1 give $\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{i=1}^nY_i)=n\sigma^2$. From [F4], scaling the centered sum by $1/n$ multiplies its variance by $1/n^2$; hence $\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=n^{-2}(n\sigma^2)=\sigma^2/n$.

The identity map on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ is measurable, so its pointwise product with itself is Borel measurable by [F3]; call this square map $q$. Applying [F4] with $q$ preserves independence. For any Borel set $B$, $\mathbb P(Y_i^2\in B)=\mathbb P(Y_i\in q^{-1}(B))$, so the common-law clause of [F2] gives a common law for the $Y_i^2$. By [F5], their common finite expectation is $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]$. Thus [F6] applies to this IID sequence and gives $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i^2\to\mathbb E[Y_1^2]$ almost surely.

Expanding the centered squares in [F1] gives $s_n^2=\frac{n}{n-1}\bigl(n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i^2-\bar Y_n^2\bigr)$. Steps 1.1 and 1.2 imply that the bracket tends almost surely to $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]-\mu^2$; also $n/(n-1)\to1$. By [F7] and [F8], $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]-\mu^2=\mathbb E[(Y_1-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2$. Hence $s_n^2\to\sigma^2$ almost surely.

If $\sigma^2>0$, step 2.1 gives $s_n^2/\sigma^2\to1$ almost surely. Both $s_n$ and $\sigma$ are nonnegative, so continuity of the square root gives $s_n/\sigma\to1$. By [F1], $\widehat{se}_n/(\sigma/\sqrt n)=s_n/\sigma$, proving the relative standard-error consistency.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.
Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid real random variables with mean $m$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then $$\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nX_k-nm}{\sigma\sqrt n}\ \Rightarrow\ N(0,1).$$

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

The map $x\mapsto\sigma x$ is continuous because $\sigma>0$. Applying [F4] to step 1.1 gives $\sigma Z_n\Rightarrow\sigma Z$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. By [A1] and [F5], the law of $\sigma Z$ is $N(0,\sigma^2)$, and $\sigma Z_n=\sqrt n(\bar Y_n-\mu)$. This is the stated convergence.

When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r < s$
([[def-rat-order]]), with rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]].

1. **In the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^{r} < a^{s}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^{r} = a^{s} = 1$; if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^{r} > a^{s}$.
2. **In the base.** If $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $r > 0$ and $0 < a < b$, then $a^{r} < b^{r}$; so $a \mapsto a^{r}$ is strictly increasing on $\{a \in \mathbb{R} : a > 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with $1$.** For rational $t > 0$: $a > 1$ implies $a^{t} > 1$, and $0 < a < 1$ implies $a^{t} < 1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

1. Let $X$ be a real random variable, let $\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let
   $F_X(x)=\mathbb P(X\le x)$. Then $F_X$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous,
   satisfies
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F_X(x)=1,$$
   and obeys
   $$\mathbb P_X((a,b])=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\qquad(a<b).$$
2. Conversely, if $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is nondecreasing and
   right-continuous with
   $$\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0,\qquad \lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1,$$
   then there is a unique Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$ such
   that
   $$\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\qquad(a<b),$$
   equivalently
   $$F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])\qquad(x\in\mathbb R).$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $f : X \to \mathbb C$ be
measurable, and let $0<p<\infty$. Then
$$\int_X |f|^p\,d\mu = p\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}\mu(\{|f|>t\})\,dt = p\int_0^\infty t^{p-1}A_f(t)\,dt,$$
where either side may be $+\infty$.

For rational $p\ne1$ and $0<A<B$,
$$\int_A^B x^{-p}\,dx=\frac{B^{1-p}-A^{1-p}}{1-p}.$$
For $p=1$ and every positive integer $N$,
$$\int_1^{2^N}\frac{dx}{x}\ge\frac N2,\qquad \int_{2^{-N}}^1\frac{dx}{x}\ge\frac N2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be a real IID sequence with $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, and set $\mu=\mathbb E[Y_1]$. Then $\mathbb E|\bar Y_n-\mu|\to0$, so $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ in probability; moreover, $\bar Y_n\to\mu$ almost surely.

Let $(Y_i)_{i\ge1}$ be real IID random variables on one probability space, where IID means that the variables have a common law and are mutually independent ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). When $\mathbb E|Y_1|<\infty$, write $\mu:=\mathbb E[Y_1]$ and define the Monte Carlo estimate of this expectation by the sample mean $\bar Y_n:=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$; this is the partial-sum convention of [[def-partial-sums-and-sample-means]]. For each $n\ge2$ and any realized finite real sample, define its sample variance and nonnegative square root by
$$s_n^2:=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\bar Y_n)^2,\qquad s_n:=\sqrt{s_n^2}.$$
When $\mathbb E[Y_1^2]<\infty$, write $\sigma^2:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1)$, using [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. The population standard error of $\bar Y_n$ is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, and its plug-in estimate is $\widehat{se}_n:=s_n/\sqrt n$. Although the finite-sample quantity $s_n$ is defined for any finite real sample, its interpretation as an estimate of a finite population standard error is used here only under the finite-second-moment condition.

derivations.claim: For $x\ge1$, $x\mapsto x^{3/2}$ is strictly increasing by [F2], so its positive reciprocal $x^{-3/2}$ is decreasing; it is continuous by [F1]. Thus the displayed $F$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous, including at $x=1$ where its two formulas agree. For $x\ge1$, [F2] gives $x^{1/2}\ge1$, hence $0\le x^{-3/2}=x^{-1}x^{-1/2}\le x^{-1}$. Since $x^{-1}\to0$, $F(x)\to1$ as $x\to+\infty$; also $F(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$. By [A1] and [F3], $F$ defines a Borel probability law $\mu$. Since $F(1)=0$, $\mu((-\infty,1])=0$ and hence $\mu([1,\infty))=1$. Restricting $\mu$ to $[1,\infty)$ gives a probability space on which the identity random variable $Y(x)=x$ is measurable by [F4], has CDF $F$, and satisfies $Y\ge1$.

If $0\le t<1$, $F(t)=0$ and hence $\mathbb P(Y>t)=1$. For $t\ge1$, the CDF gives $\mathbb P(Y>t)=1-F(t)=t^{-3/2}$. By the nonnegative expectation definition [F5] and layer-cake formula [F6], $\mathbb E[Y]=1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3/2}\,dt$. The function $t^{-3/2}$ is nonnegative and continuous on every compact $[1,R]$ by [F1]. For $R>1$, [F8] gives $\int_1^R t^{-3/2}\,dt=2(1-R^{-1/2})\to2$; [F9] identifies this finite improper integral with its Lebesgue value. Therefore $\mathbb E[Y]=3$.

Since $Y\ge1$ on the restricted space, $\mathbb P(|Y|>t)=\mathbb P(Y>t)$. By the nonnegative expectation definition [F5] and [F7] with $p=2$, $\mathbb E[Y^2]=1+2\int_1^\infty t^{-1/2}\,dt$. Extend $h(t)=t^{-1/2}$ from $[1,\infty)$ by $h(t)=1$ for $t<1$; it is continuous at $1$ and on both pieces, so [F11] makes it Borel. Since $[1,N]$ is Borel, [F12] makes each $h\mathbf1_{[1,N]}$ measurable. For each integer $N\ge2$, [F1] gives continuity of $t^{-1/2}$ on $[1,N]$, and [F8] and [F10] give $\int_{[1,N]}t^{-1/2}\,d\lambda=2(\sqrt N-1)$. These values diverge because the natural numbers are unbounded. The truncations increase pointwise to $t^{-1/2}\mathbf1_{[1,\infty)}$, so [F13] gives $\int_{[1,\infty)}t^{-1/2}\,d\lambda=+\infty$. Hence $\mathbb E[Y^2]=+\infty$.

For any IID sequence with this law, step 2.1 gives a finite first absolute moment, so [F14] proves strong and weak consistency of $\bar Y_n$. Step 3.1 shows the finite-second-moment condition in [F15] fails; therefore this contract gives no finite $\sigma$ or finite $\sigma/\sqrt n$ standard error. The empirical formula remains a finite-sample statistic by [F15].
